source: Minchat Shai on Gen 24:22 (the Masorah: 'לשתת — FOUR defective; their signs: until they finish drinking; they could not drink of the Nile; Marah; Rephidim'; the Ramah concurs)
claim_en: THE FOUR LEAN DRINKS: לשתת ('to drink,' defective) stands exactly FOUR times in the Torah, and they are precisely the Masorah's four — Rebecca's own offer ('until they have finished TO DRINK,' 24:19) and the three water-crises: the undrinkable Nile (Exod 7:24), Marah's bitterness (Exod 15:23), waterless Rephidim (Exod 17:1). The maiden's lean drink-word keeps company with the wilderness thirsts.
middah: ink (the written form — the Masorah's note)

source: Minchat Shai on Gen 24:22 ('when the camels had finished TO DRINK — plene vav in the precise books, the Hilleli, the old prints')
claim_en: ...and three verses later the narrator writes the same infinitive PLENE: כלו לשתות ('the camels had FINISHED drinking,' 24:22) — the offer lean, the fulfillment full, inside one scene, exactly as the precise books and the Hilleli rule against the printers.
middah: ink (the written form — the Masorah's note)

source: Minchat Shai on Gen 24:8 ('EVERY oath-noun in the Torah defective of vav — for every oath is from the word SEVEN'; Shaarei Orah, the second gate, cited: Abraham's seven ewes at Beer Sheva)
claim_en: THE OATH IS ALWAYS SEVEN: משבעתי ('you shall be clear of THIS MY OATH,' 24:8) — the oath-noun runs DEFECTIVE through the whole Torah (all ten tokens, builder-asserted lean), 'for every oath is from the word seven' (Shaarei Orah via Minchat Shai): the letters keep the oath indistinguishable from the seven — as at Beer Sheva, where the seven ewes sealed the swearing (21:28-31, the frozen well-oath unit).
middah: ink (the written form — the Masorah's note)

source: Minchat Shai on Gen 24:14 ('הנערה is READ' — the qere note; the Zohar page named); the Masorah's Torah-wide maiden-rule
claim_en: THE MAIDEN WRITTEN AS THE LAD: הנער — at Rebecca's debut ('let THE MAIDEN to whom I say...,' 24:14) the consonants are the BOY-skeleton (no final heh) carrying GIRL-vowels: written one sex, read the other. SNAPSHOT instruments the whole rule: the vowel-only feminine skeleton stands at EIGHT Torah tokens (Rebecca's five in this chapter, Dinah's three in Gen 34, builder-asserted); the maiden-laws of Deut 22 pair an unpointed ktiv-token with its read-form; and in the WHOLE TORAH exactly ONE maiden is written out in full — Deut 22:19, where the slanderer must keep his bride ('she shall remain his wife'): the one place the letter writes her whole.
middah: ink (the written form — the Masorah's note)

source: Bereshit Rabbah 65:9
claim_en: AN INK CLAIM OPENED UNDER GUARD 3, AND IT DOES NOT SURVIVE OUR TREE. The chain holds that aging is not written from the beginning of the book until this point - 'when Abraham stood, He granted him aging: Abraham was old' - reading 24:1 as the first-aging seat and the head of a three-demands ladder. Machine-checked against our corpus, the claim fails on its own terms: the word stands five times before this verse, at 18:11, 18:12, 18:13, 19:4 and 19:31, and 18:11 carries the very phrase - old, advanced in days - that 24:1 repeats. The census is recorded as the chain's own premise and is NOT applied to our tree; the counter-witness at 18:11 is machine-checked and carried with it. The ladder's other rungs stand or fall separately.
middah: ink (the chain's first-aging premise against the corpus's own count — five earlier seats; recorded, not applied)

source: Bereshit Rabbah 59:6
claim_en: THE WORD FOR OLD IS READ AS AN ABBREVIATION OF A SENTENCE. 'Old' is taken as standing for 'this one ACQUIRED' - two worlds acquired - and the verse's second phrase, advanced in days, as entry into both. Around it the chain builds a three-crowned census of those crowned with age AND with days, each the head of a line, and R. Acha's correspondence rule: the appearance of age and the count of days can come apart, and in Abraham they matched.

check.note: A single word read as a compressed sentence, generating a census of comparable figures.

middah: E30 (old read as this-one-acquired — the word as a sentence's abbreviation)

source: Bereshit Rabbah 59:7
claim_en: 'WITH EVERYTHING' IS A FOUR-WAY RECORDED DISPUTE, AND ONE LEG CLOSES A PRIOR BLOCK. What Abraham was blessed with is argued and left argued: R. Yudan says a daughter; R. Nechemya denies any daughter at all, against the king's-household objection; R. Levi offers three - rule over his own inclination, Ishmael repenting in his lifetime, and a storehouse that lacked nothing; and R. Chama in Levi's name says He did not test him again. That last leg converges with the oath the machine already records at 22:16 in gen_38, reached from a different verse by a different argument. The Ishmael-repentance leg is spent forward at 25:9 and 25:17 in gen_42.

check.note: An unresolved multi-way dispute whose legs wire backward and forward to other blocks' operators.

middah: plain (a teacher's statement — an identification, a narrative expansion, a recorded dispute, or the verse's own wording read as the rule; no catalogued inference form)

source: Bereshit Rabbah 59:8
claim_en: THE OATH-OBJECT IS READ AS A PROCEDURE. R. Berekhya reads the hand under the thigh as an oath taken by the sign of the covenant: because it was given through pain it is beloved, and 'they would take an oath only by it'. A gesture in a narrative is thereby converted into the standing form of a procedure - what one swears BY, and why that object and no other.

check.note: A narrative gesture read as fixing the object of a legal procedure.

middah: plain (the hand under the thigh as the oath's procedure)

source: Bereshit Rabbah 59:8
claim_en: A THEOLOGY BUILT ON THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN TWO VERSES OF ONE SPEECH. R. Pinchas rides the ink: at 24:3 Abraham swears by the God of the heavens AND the God of the earth, and four verses later at 24:7 he says only God of the heavens. The difference is read as biography - before Abraham made Him known He was of the heavens only, and Abraham MADE Him God of the earth. Machine-checked: the second divine title is present at 24:3 and absent at 24:7, so the claim rides a real feature of our own ink, not a paraphrase.
middah: M-23 (God of the heavens and the earth at 24:3 against God of the heavens alone at 24:7 — the drop read as biography)

source: Bereshit Rabbah 59:10
claim_en: THE OATH'S PREAMBLE IS PARSED AS A REGISTRY OF PRIOR EVENTS. Each clause of 24:7 is assigned a seat: 'who took me from my father's house' is the house, 'from the land of my birth' the neighbourhood, 'who swore to me' the oath in Charan, and 'who spoke to me' the covenant between the pieces - so gen_31's covenant is named as the standing oath-seat this verse refers back to. The restrictive particle is read as an exclusion that reaches a generation further than it says: the son may not return, and the grandson does not either.

check.note: A verse's relative clauses mapped one-to-one onto earlier recorded events, with a restriction extended by inference.

middah: plain (each clause of 24:7 assigned its prior event; the restrictive only read a generation further, E2, beside)

source: Onkelos Genesis 24:3
claim_en: THE OATH IS ROUTED THROUGH THE WORD. Where the verse has Abraham swear BY THE LORD, Onkelos has him swear by the WORD of the LORD - the same buffer the machine already carries at the Beersheba covenant in gen_37. Set beside the chain's thigh-oath reading on the adjacent verse, one oath scene ends with two different accounts of what is sworn by: an object in the midrash, a mediating Word in the translation.

check.note: The reverence buffer supplying an oath-object that the midrash leg supplies differently.

middah: ink (the received translation's rendering)

source: Bereshit Rabbah 60:3; Mishnah Temurah 5:6
claim_en: THE SERVANT'S OPEN CONDITION IS ENROLLED IN A VOID-VOW CLASS. Four are named who asked improperly - this servant, Caleb, Saul, and Yiftach - of whom three were answered properly and one was not. The law layer is quoted with the narrative: the dispute over monetary consecration, and the received ruling that one who declares an impure or blemished animal a burnt offering HAS SAID NOTHING, voiding the class. The chain then records the standoff in which neither Pinchas nor Yiftach would go to the other, both punished, each punishment proved from ink. A conditional in a narrative is being tested against a case table.

check.note: A narrative conditional classed against a testing-shelf ruling that voids the vow type.

middah: plain (a teacher's statement — an identification, a narrative expansion, a recorded dispute, or the verse's own wording read as the rule; no catalogued inference form)

source: Bereshit Rabbah 60:4
claim_en: A THREE-MEMBER CENSUS OF PRAYERS ANSWERED BEFORE THEY FINISHED. R. Shimon ben Yochai counts three: this servant, whose sign arrives 'before he had finished speaking'; Moses, where the ground split as he ended; and Solomon, where the fire came down. Our verse is the class's first member, and the class is defined by a timing feature of the narration rather than by content.

check.note: A census whose membership test is narrative timing, not subject matter.

middah: plain (a teacher's statement — an identification, a narrative expansion, a recorded dispute, or the verse's own wording read as the rule; no catalogued inference form)

source: Bereshit Rabbah 60:6
claim_en: THE BETROTHAL GIFTS ARE READ AS A FORESHADOWING BY WEIGHT AND COUNT. The nose-ring of half a shekel is read to the census half-shekel, the TWO bracelets to the two tablets, and their TEN of gold to the ten commandments. The gifts of one betrothal scene are made to carry the numbers of a later covenant, so a courtship inventory doubles as a typology.

check.note: Object weights and counts in a narrative read as numeric anticipations of a later event.

source: Bereshit Rabbah 59:11; Bereshit Rabbah 60:8; Onkelos Genesis 24:11
claim_en: ONE VERB, THREE READINGS, AND A COLLISION INSIDE THE DECLARED SHELF. The midrash reads that he made the camels KNEEL; Onkelos refuses the kneel-and-bless homograph and renders that he made them REST. Beside it the chain disputes itself about the animals: that he untied their MUZZLES - Abraham's camels going out muzzled as a theft-prevention signature - against R. Huna and R. Yirmeya, who object from the doctrine that the patriarch's animals would not graze a stolen field, citing the donkey that refused untithed barley and the received ruling exempting animal feed from doubtfully-tithed produce. Both poles are recorded; neither wins.

check.note: One narrative verb read three ways, with an internal doctrinal collision preserved unresolved.

middah: plain (a teacher's statement — an identification, a narrative expansion, a recorded dispute, or the verse's own wording read as the rule; no catalogued inference form)

source: Bereshit Rabbah 60:8
claim_en: THE TRADITION MEASURES ITS OWN INK ECONOMY AND STATES THE RULE OUT LOUD. R. Acha holds that the conversation of the patriarchs' household servants is more significant than the descendants' Torah: this servant's errand spans columns and is then REPEATED in full, while a whole law of impurity hangs on a single extra letter - the added definite letter in 'the impure' on one opinion, the joining letter of 'and this' on another. The chain is comparing the cost of its own text against the yield, and the observation governs how the repetition block that follows should be read.

check.note: A stated meta-rule about textual economy, offered as the reason a long repetition is permitted to stand.

middah: plain (the ink-economy meta-rule — the servants' conversation against a law on one letter)

source: Onkelos Genesis 24:21
claim_en: AN EMOTION IS RENDERED AS TEST PROCEDURE. Where the verse says the man was astonished at her, Onkelos renders that he WAITED AND OBSERVED SILENTLY to determine - the inner state replaced by an observation protocol. The midrash leg arrives near the same place by a different route, reading the verb as squinting to determine. The translation de-psychologizes; the chain keeps the person and adds the scrutiny.

check.note: An interior state rendered as an observational procedure by the translation.

middah: ink (the received translation's rendering)

source: Bereshit Rabbah 60:9
claim_en: A DISCLOSURE RULE DERIVED FROM THE ORDER OF THE SERVANT'S WORDS. That he will not eat until he has spoken, and that his first words are 'I am Abraham's servant', yield R. Yitzchak's rule that a man states his own flaw first - disclosure before negotiation. The sequence of a narrative speech is read as the required order of a procedure.

check.note: Speech order in a narrative read as a disclosure requirement.

middah: M-11 (the servant's first words before his meal — disclosure before negotiation; Bereshit Rabbah 60:9)
